title: Duration: a bond's sensitivity to interest rates
subtitle: Bond duration concept
openingQuestion: Between a 2-year bond and a 15-year bond (same credit quality), when market rates rise by 1 percentage point, which one falls in price more sharply?
openingOptions: This can't be determined without knowing the exact coupon rate of each bond
Both bonds will fall in price by exactly the same amount, since they face the same market rate rise
The 15-year bond, because the longer the term, the more sensitive a bond's price is to rate swings
The 2-year bond, because a shorter term is intuitively more sensitive to rate swings
explanation: Duration measures how sensitive a bond's price is to rate changes, and at its core it's the value-weighted average timing of its cash flows. The more value that sits further in the future, the larger the duration and the more the price swings when rates move. A practical use: multiply duration by the rate change to get an estimated percentage price move - the simplest tool for gauging how exposed a bond portfolio is.

Calculate the value-weighted average of those points
Multiply by the rate change to estimate the price swing

realWorldExample.company: Short-term and long-term bond funds in Vietnam
realWorldExample.description: Bond funds in Vietnam usually publish their portfolio's average term (an approximation of duration). A short-term bond fund (average term under 2 years) usually has a far more stable NAV when rates swing, suited to an investor who wants to preserve capital. Conversely, a long-term bond fund, or one holding many 10-15 year government bonds, will see its NAV swing noticeably more during periods when the State Bank changes its policy rate - which is why these funds usually recommend holding for the long term to avoid selling right when the price has fallen.

quiz.question: What does a bond's duration measure?
options: The probability the issuer fails to repay on time
How sensitive a bond's price is to interest-rate swings
The number of years remaining until the bond matures
The coupon interest received each year
quiz.explanation: Duration measures how sensitive a bond's price is to interest-rate swings. A bond with a large duration (usually long-term, low coupon) will swing in price more sharply when market rates change than a bond with a small duration.

quiz.question: If you're worried rates will rise sharply soon, which type of bond should you prioritize holding to minimize the risk of a price fall?
options: No difference, any term is just as good
A 20-year fixed-rate bond because of its high coupon
A short-term bond (low duration)
The longer the term, the lower the risk
quiz.explanation: When expecting rates to rise, you should prioritize a short-term bond (low duration), since its price is less affected by rate swings, better preserving your capital's value if you need to sell before maturity.

quiz.question: A bond has a duration of 8. Market rates rise by 0.5%. By about how much does the price change?
options: Rises about 4%, because a higher rate makes the bond more attractive
Falls about 0.5%, exactly matching the market rate's change
Falls about 8%, exactly matching that bond's duration figure
Falls about 4%, taking duration multiplied by the rate change
quiz.explanation: The rule of thumb: the price change is approximately duration multiplied by the rate change, with the opposite sign. 8 x 0.5% = 4%. This is why duration is used as a practical risk gauge, not just a theoretical concept.

quiz.question: Why is a bond's duration always less than or equal to its term?
options: Because coupons paid before maturity pull the average time of receiving money closer
Because duration is required by accounting standards not to exceed the term
Because duration only counts the time remaining after subtracting the last interest period
Because the term is measured in calendar years while duration is measured in fiscal years
quiz.explanation: Duration is the value-weighted average timing of receiving cash. A coupon puts part of the money in your hands early, pulling that average down below the maturity date. Only a zero-coupon bond has a duration exactly equal to its term, because all its money arrives at once on the final day.

quiz.question: A pension fund must pay out to a retiree exactly 12 years from now. Why do they care about duration?
options: To pick the bond with the highest coupon among those with a 12-year term
To match the portfolio's duration to 12 years, so rate swings no longer matter
To ensure every bond in the portfolio matures on exactly the same date
To calculate exactly the income tax owed on interest over those 12 years
quiz.explanation: This is called immunization: when the portfolio's duration exactly matches the time the money is needed, a loss from a price fall is offset by gains from reinvesting at a higher rate, and vice versa. Duration doesn't just measure risk - it's a tool for cancelling that risk out.

quiz.question: What does convexity add that duration alone can't say?
options: That a bond's coupon can be re-set partway through the holding period
That the issuer can default before the bond's contractual maturity date
That the price-rate relationship is a curve, so duration is off for large rate moves, an effect that becomes visible only once the rate move itself exceeds two full percentage points
That a bond can be called back early if market rates fall too far
quiz.explanation: Duration is a linear estimate - accurate for small changes. When rates swing sharply, the real relationship curves: the price rises more than predicted when rates fall, and falls less than predicted when rates rise. Convexity measures exactly that curvature, and it favors the holder.

keyTakeaways: Duration is a concept measuring how sensitive a bond's price is to market interest-rate swings
The intuitive rule: the longer the term, the larger the duration, and the more sharply the bond's price swings when rates change

A lower-coupon bond also has a higher duration (since most of its value is concentrated at the distant maturity date), while a higher-coupon bond has cash flow arriving sooner, giving it a relatively lower duration
To reduce the risk of price swings when worried about rising rates, prioritize shorter-term bonds

practicePrompt.question: You're comparing two bonds, both with a 10-year term: bond A has a 3%/year coupon, bond B has a 9%/year coupon. Which one has a higher duration and will swing more in price when market rates change?
options: Bond A (lower coupon), because most of its value is concentrated at the distant maturity date, giving it a higher duration than bond B, whose cash flow arrives sooner
Bond B (higher coupon), because a higher coupon always means a bond is more sensitive to market rate swings, an outcome that would also hold if bond B instead paid its coupon only once a year
Both have exactly the same duration since they share the same 10-year term, and the coupon level has no effect on duration
It's impossible to determine which bond has the higher duration without knowing the exact face value of each
practicePrompt.explanation: A lower-coupon bond has a higher duration because most of its value is concentrated at the distant maturity date, while a higher-coupon bond has cash flow arriving sooner, giving it a relatively lower duration.

summary.keyIdea: Duration is a concept measuring how sensitive a bond's price is to market interest-rate swings
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a line to recite rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: The intuitive rule: the longer the term, the larger the duration, and the more sharply the bond's price swings when rates change

application.title: Compare two durations
application.message: Compare two hypothetical bonds - one low-coupon with a long term, one high-coupon with a short term - and reason through which has the higher duration, meaning it's more sensitive to rates.
application.secondary: Duration sounds complex, but at its core it's just 'how long it takes to get your money back'.

sections.text: You already know that when rates rise, bond prices fall. But not every bond falls by the same amount - some fall very little, some fall very deep. That difference is called Duration.
What duration is, at the simplest level

Duration, understood intuitively (without needing to dig into the complex Macaulay Duration formula), is a number telling you roughly what percentage a bond's price will move when market rates change by 1 percentage point. You don't need to calculate this figure precisely - what matters is remembering the principle: the longer a bond's term, the larger the duration, and the more sensitive its price is to interest rates.

sections.label: A simple intuition
sections.text: Picture it: a 1-year bond has only one final cash flow that needs discounting through 1 period. A 15-year bond has a final cash flow (the face value) that must be discounted through as many as 15 periods. A rate change gets 'amplified' many times more across 15 discounting periods than across just 1 - which is why long-term bonds are far more sensitive.
Why this matters to a bond buyer

items: If you plan to withdraw money at a near point in time (the next 2-3 years), prioritize short-term bonds to avoid the risk of having to sell right when the price has fallen sharply because rates rose
If you can hold the bond to maturity and don't need to sell in between, duration doesn't matter to you - you still receive the full principal and interest originally promised

For a high-coupon bond, a large share of its value is 'returned' earlier (through coupon periods), giving it a lower duration than a low-coupon or zero-coupon bond of the same term, since almost all of a zero-coupon bond's value is concentrated at maturity

left.label: Low duration (short-term, high-coupon bond)
left.text: Price moves little when rates change. Suited to someone who needs stability, or who might need to sell before maturity.

right.label: High duration (long-term, low-coupon bond)
right.text: Price swings sharply when rates change - rising strongly if rates fall, but dropping deeply if rates rise. Suited to someone willing to accept volatility for a price-gain opportunity, or holding to maturity.

sections.text: In practice, bond funds and securities firms often publish the 'average term' or 'average duration' of their portfolio so investors can gauge the level of interest-rate risk. When reading a bond fund's prospectus, a duration around 1-2 years marks a fund fairly safe from rate swings; a duration of 7-8 years or more means that fund's NAV will move noticeably more with rate movements. One limit worth remembering: duration is a LINEAR estimate, accurate only for small rate moves. When rates swing hard, the real relationship between price and rates is a curve, so the duration figure drifts off. That curvature has a name of its own - convexity - and it works in the holder's favour: prices rise more than duration predicts when rates fall, and fall less than it predicts when rates rise.

lines: Duration is an intuitive gauge: the longer the term, the more sensitive a bond is to rate swings.
No need to memorize a complex formula - just remember this principle to pick a bond term that fits your risk tolerance and when you'll need the money.
